appraisal_events.evidence: « Oui, oui, tu peux continuer », dit-elle ironiquement « en esquissant le geste de quelqu'un qui vous fait la barbe » ; elle vante le danseur (« il est épatant avec ses mains ») puis lui montre « les traits convulsés de Robert » : « Regarde, il souffre. »
appraisal_events.explanation: Rachel dismisses Saint-Loup's ultimatum as empty noise, publicly prefers the dancer to him, and exhibits his visible pain to a third party as a spectacle; the narrator's framing (convulsed features, sadistic cruelty) confirms that Saint-Loup is humiliated and powerless in the exchange.

status_effects.explanation: Saint-Loup is locally reduced to visible suffering under a woman who controls the scene; his agony is displayed to a rival rather than answered.
His solemn, irrevocable break speech is drained of force: Rachel meets it with a mocking gesture, and the narrator undercuts it further with a merely conditional « Peut-être était-il sincère ».
Rachel holds complete leverage: she chooses the tone, redirects attention to the dancer, and can display her lover's pain at will.

ambiguities: The woman is never named in the passage (only « elle », « sa maîtresse »); the identification as Rachel rests on the surrounding scene and prior context rather than on any surface name in the text itself.

The narrator qualifies the cruelty twice — it is an « élan momentané » « nullement en rapport avec ses vrais sentiments d'affection pour Saint-Loup », and Saint-Loup's ultimatum is only « peut-être » sincere — leaving open whether this is a stable dominance or a passing impulse within a mutually attached couple.
